background.definition: TSC is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome with variable phenotypic expression. It is characterized by the development of hamartomas in multiple organ systems including the skin, brain, eyes, heart, liver, lungs, and kidney. Clinical manifestations may include characteristic skin tumors, seizures, and developmental delays.

list.listitem: From 1 in 6000 to 1 in 25,000 live births.
Using a provincial health-care database in Quebec, 1,004 subjects with TSC were identified, for a prevalence of one in 7,872 people.
Two tumor suppressor genes have been identified as the cause of TSC; mutations can be inherited or, in the case of two-thirds of the patients, sporadic.
TSC1, located on chromosome 9q34, codes for hamartin.
TSC2, located on chromosome 16p13.3, codes for tuberin.

About 70% to 80% of patients who meet definite criteria for TSC present with the TSC1 or TSC2 mutation; the remainder have large gene deletions, somatic mosaic mutations, and mutations in noncoding gene regions.
The proteins hamartin and tuberin regulate cell growth and tumorigenesis.
An interaction between hamartin and tuberin forms a tumor suppressor TSC1/TSC2 heterodimer inhibiting the activity of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR).

The TSC1/TSC2 heterodimer contains a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that inactives GTP-bound Rheb to a GDP-bound Rheb. Rheb, a G protein, in its active state stimulates mTOR. mTOR in turn phosphorylates 2 target proteins, S6K1 and 4E-BP1, which promote protein synthesis and cell growth.
Therefore, inactivation of mTOR leads to cell growth arrest. The TSC1 or TSC2 mutations can lead to dysregulation of this pathway if there is a mutation in the GAP domain.
Screen family members with an affected child to evaluate for subtle disease and for genetic counseling. C

Screening includes full-body skin examination with UV light, retinal examination with dilated pupils, cranial CT (preferred) or cranial MRI, renal ultrasonography, and molecular diagnostic methods if available. C
Consider TSC if a patient presents with epilepsy, cardiac dysfunction, or hypomelanotic macules. C
Diagnostic criteria are divided into major and minor features (). Depending on how many features the individual has, they are diagnosed as having definite, probable, or possible TSC. C

At the time of diagnosis, neurodevelopmental and ophthalmic tests, ECG, renal ultrasonography, cranial CT, or MRI should be completed. If cardiac symptoms and seizures occur, echocardiography and EEG should be considered.C
DNA testing identifies a specific gene abnormality in about 80% of cases. C

Differential.Differential_Features: No accentuation of nevus under UV light
Demonstrates an off-white accentuation under UV light similar to TSC; no other features of TSC
Acquired and progressive; chalky-white accentuation under UV light
Genetic testing will reveal a MEN-1 gene mutation

list.listitem: Patients can present with dermatologic, neurologic, renal, pulmonary, cardiovascular, and ocular manifestations. Consider TSC if a patient presents with epilepsy, cardiac dysfunction, or hypomelanotic macules.
Hypomelanotic macules, known as Fitzpatrick patches or "ash leaf" spots (97%): leaf-shaped or polygonal, commonly found on the trunk and buttock, and usually present at birth or infancy.

Facial angiofibromas (75%): red-pink papules, distribution over the centrofacial lip areas, sparing the central upper lip; present during the second to fifth year of life and becoming more prominent with age.

Shagreen patches (48%): a connective tissue hamartoma that presents as a patch or plaques with a rough surface resembling an orange peel, distributed on the dorsal body surface, especially over the lumbosacral region; rarely present in infancy, increasing in number and size with age.
Molluscum pendulum (23%): multiple soft pedunculated growths usually found on the neck; rarely present in infancy, seen during the 1st decade of life.
Forehead fibrous plaques (19%): yellow-brown or skin-colored plaques usually located on the forehead and scalp; can be present at birth or infancy, but common at any age.

Periungual fibromas (15%): reddish or skin-colored plaques commonly found on toes along the lateral nail groove, nail plate, or proximal nail folds; onset usually at puberty, becoming more common with age.
"Confetti-like" macules (3%): multiple, 1- to 2-mm white spots distributed symmetrically over the extremities; usually present during adulthood or the second decade of life.
Brain hamartomas including cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas.
Seizures (over 90%): most are infantile spasms followed by generalized seizures. The first seizure occurs in the first 2 years of life in 85% of patients.
Behavioral and cognitive dysfunction (40%-55%): includes developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism.
Angiomyolipomas (69%): less common in young age, increasing incidence with age; most do not cause complications or symptoms, but bleeding can occur in growths larger than 3 cm.

Renal cysts (30%) (also found in polycystic kidney disease ([PKD]): can be found in 5% of patients. The TSC2 gene is located 48 base pairs away from the PKD1 gene; therefore, a contiguous deletion can lead to the manifestation of both TSC and PKD in the same individual.
Renal cell carcinoma (1%).
Pulmonary lesions (1%-6%). Women of child-bearing age may present with progressive dyspnea or spontaneous pneumothorax.

The most common lesion is lymphangiomyomatosis (LAM), characterized by a proliferation of abnormal smooth muscle-like LAM cells leading to cystic lung lesions and pneumothorax. In the Quebec database, 9 of 38 subjects with LAM also had TCS.

Cardiac rhabdomyomas (48%-60%): 65% of patients less than 2 years of age have this manifestation. These tumors usually regress with age, although some have been reported to grow around puberty, and are for the most part asymptomatic. However, cardiac insufficiency, heart failure, murmurs, and arrhythmias (commonly Wolf-Parkinson-White) have been reported.
Retinal astrocytic hamartomas (40%-44%): usually stable over time. The translucent, flat lesion is the most common type, followed by the multinodular "mulberry" lesion.
Angiofibroma of the eyelids reported in up to 39% of patients.

Evaluate individual to determine definite, probable, or possible fulfillment of diagnostic criteria. This includes personal and family history, full-body skin examination, including use of a Wood's light, fundoscopy, cranial imaging with CT scan or MRI, renal ultrasound, and echocardiography in infants.

Infants with diagnosed TSC may be considered for EEG screening in the absence of seizures; epileptiform discharges that do not amount to full seizures may be treated with vigabatrin to improve intellectual outcomes.

Order EEG if seizures are present, and urgent cranial CT or MRI if patients present with signs of intracranial pressure (ICP) or focal neurologic signs. Diffusion tensor imaging may be helpful for identifying epileptogenic tubers.
An ECG and echocardiogram are indicated if arrhythmias or loss of consciousness is present.
Order spirometry and chest x-ray for initial evaluation of pulmonary symptoms, followed in most cases by chest CT.

Molecular genetic testing can be performed in the patient as well as family members to detect familial or sporadic mutations. If a familial mutation is detected, genetic counseling can help assess the chances of having another child with the same disease. In cases of mosaicism (2%-3%), the mutation may not be apparent in the DNA testing. Future children may still be affected.

Based on findings of the 2021 International Tuberous Sclerosis Complex Clinical Consensus Conference, a definite diagnosis of TSC is defined as the presence of at least 2 major features or 1 major and 2 or more minor features; in addition, a pathological mutation in TSC1 or TSC2 is diagnostic. Diagnostic criteria are given in .
The testing recommendations are summarized in (adapted from ).
Initiate vigabatrin therapy for epileptic discharges seen on EEG, even in the absence of seizures, to improve developmental outcomes. A
For infantile spasm, vigabatrin is a first-line treatment; A topiramate, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, and levetiracetam can also be used. C
Vagal nerve stimulation and a ketogenic diet can also be used to decrease seizure frequency. B
For intractable seizures, increased ICP, or giant cell astrocytomas, resection should be considered. B
The first-line treatment of renal hemorrhages related to angiomyolipoma is selective arterial embolization. B
Consider laser therapy and excision in the treatment of facial angiofibroma and ungual fibromas, respectively. C
Sirolimus or everolimus treatment have been shown to be effective in the treatment of astrocytomas and may also benefit other TSC manifestations such as facial angiofibromas.B

Initiate vigabatrin therapy for epileptic discharges seen on EEG, even in the absence of seizures, to improve developmental outcomes. The epilepsy associated with TSC does not respond to standard treatment in >50% of cases.
For infantile spasm-type seizures, vigabatrin therapy has been shown to be effective.
Other antiepileptic medications that have been shown to be effective are topiramate, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, and levetiracetam.

The efficacy of oral cannabidiol added to usual care was assessed in an RCT of 224 patients (average age 11.4 years) with treatment-resistant seizures and tuberous sclerosis. Patients who received 50 mg/kg/day or 25 mg/kg/day of oral CBD had fewer seizures after 16 weeks than those randomized to placebo (47.5%, 48.6%, and 26.5% reduction from baseline, respectively). Discontinuation due to adverse effects was more common in the CBD groups (8, 10, and 2 patients, respectively). A continuation of the same study for safety outcomes found continued seizure reduction and a majority of patients reporting adverse effects, but 75% continuing the medication.

Topical sirolimus is an mTOR inhibitor and has been studied in the treatment of TSC at serum levels of 5 to 15 ng/mL and has been shown to induce astrocytoma regression. Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 prospective nonrandomized studies involving 94 patients treated with sirolimus found a size reduction of angiomyolipoma in 46.8% in the first year and 43.5% (20/46) of those still being treated in the second year. Treatment was discontinued in 5% of 40 treated in the second year; adverse reactions included stomatitis, respiratory infection, skin lesions and hyperlipidemia.

Topical sirolimus diminishes facial angiofibromas and hypomelanotic macules.A left-right comparative study of sirolimus 0.2% topical gel in 11 patients found significant improvement over a 12-week period. The improvement appears to be greater in younger patients. In a small RCT, 0.2% topical sirolimus was also shown to improve facial angiofibromas at 12 weeks compared to lower doses; side effects were minor, with skin dryness and irritation in about one third.
A shelf-stabilized version of topical sirolimus was found to be effective in a randomized trial.

In an RCT of 118 patients with TSC-associated angiomyolipomas from 24 centers in 11 countries, those randomized to everolimus had a response rate of 42% (33 of 79 [95% CI 31%–53%]) vs. 0% (0 of 39 [0–9%]) for placebo. The most common adverse events were stomatitis (48% vs. 8% for placebo), nasopharyngitis (24% vs. 31% for placebo), and acne-like skin lesions (22% vs. 5%).

In a follow-up study of 8 children taking everolimus for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, 5 of whom had drug-resistant epilepsy at baseline, 6 had at least a 50% reduction in tumor volume. One child with drug-resistant epilepsy had cessation of seizures and 2 others experienced at least a 50% reduction in the number of seizures.

Adjunctive everolimus was demonstrated to be effective in reducing seizure frequency by >50% in a 3-arm RCT with 366 patients aged 2-65 years with TSC and treatment-resistant seizures. Patients randomized to low-exposure and high-exposure everolimus had a higher response rate of 28.2% (95% CI 20.3-37.3) and 40% (95% CI 31.5-49.0), respectively, compared to 15.1% with placebo (95% CI 9.2-22.8). Adverse events leading to discontinuation occurred in six (5%) patients in the low-exposure group, four (3%) in the high-exposure group, and two (2%) patients in the placebo group.
In a follow-up study of 18 patients with TSC and medically-refractory epilepsy, 13 of 14 completing the study reported improved seizure control at 4 years with everolimus.

In a case series of everolimus in 18 children under age 3 years, adverse effects including stomatitis, cough, pharyngitis, and pyrexia occurred in all children; however, serious adverse drug effects occurred in only 4 children and only one discontinued medication due to an adverse reaction (acinetobacter bacteremia).

A trial randomized 52 patients with TSC and facial angiofibromas to topical rapamycin-calcitriol or either agent alone in a split-face comparison. Rapamycin and rapamycin-calcitriol were similarly effective based on a symptom score, but the combination worked faster and had better durability after discontinuation.

Neurosurgical interventions for intractable seizures, increased intracranial pressure, and giant cell astrocytomas include focal resections, lobectomy, multilobar resection, hemispherectomy, and corpus callosotomy. One study showed that 57% of patients were free of seizures during a 3.7-year follow-up and that seizure frequency improved by more than 90% in 18% of patients.
A systematic review of 40 studies with 1157 patients found excellent seizure reduction in 59% and worthwhile or excellent seizure reductions in 85%.
Vagal nerve stimulation demonstrated at least a 50% reduction in seizure frequency in 90% of patients and a 90% reduction in 50% of patients.
Selective arterial embolization for renal hemorrhage is used in angiomyolipoma.
Excision of ungual fibromas is the treatment of choice.
Laser treatment is recommended for facial angiofibromas.

A ketogenic diet consisting of a 3:1 or 4:1 fat to carbohydrate ratio was shown to cause a 50% reduction in seizures in 92% of children; 67% of patients had a response rate of more than 90% when the diet was instituted for a mean of 2 years.
Many patients with TSC have complex needs and require comanagement with specialists.
Refer to a specialist if frank hematuria exists or if a renal ultrasound reveals a solid renal lesion with low fat content.
Also refer for surgical management of refractory seizures and increased ICP due to hydrocephalus, which is may be caused by a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma.
Infantile spasm may indicate worse intellectual outcomes when seen on initial examination.
Developmental and behavioral problems such as autism and attention deficit disorder are commonly comorbid with TSC. Developmental testing should be recommended annually.
Although the mortality rate has been reported to be as high as 40% by the age of 35 years, with appropriate medical care, most patients experience a normal life span.

In a study of 355 patients with TSC examined at the Mayo Clinic, 49 died; 9 of causes other than TSC. Causes of death included 11 from renal disease, 10 from brain tumors, and 4 of lymphangiomyomatosis of the lung.
See Table 2 for recommended follow-up tests.

Assess development including pervasive developmental disorders, at least annually. Screening should be comprehensive (such as through early intervention or a formal developmental program for older children).
Consider EEG surveillance for infants <24 months diagnosed with TSC without known seizure disorder.
Monitor blood pressure annually. Order UA, electrolytes, and serum creatinine in children and adults. Order renal ultrasound annually if lesions are present.
A patient-reported outcome measurement tool for tuberous sclerosis has been validated. Subscales include physical function, mental functions, and social support, among others.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Tuberous Sclerosis.
feature.feature_body:
Definite tuberous sclerosis (TSC): 2 major features or 1 major feature and 2 minor features. Possible TSC: 1 major feature or 2 or more minor features. Major features
Ungual fibromas (≥ 2). Hypomelanotic macule (≥3; at least 5mm). Shagreen patch (connective tissue nevus). Multiple retinal hamartomas. Multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines. Subependymal nodule (≥ 2). Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma. Cardiac rhabdomyoma (single or multiple). Lymphangiomyomatosis. Angiofibroma (≥3) or fibrous cephalic plaque Minor features
Dental enamel pits (≥ 3). "Confetti" skin lesions Intraoral fibromas (≥ 2). Nonrenal hamartomas. Retinal achromic patch. "Confetti" skin lesions. Multiple renal cysts.
From Northrup H, Aronow ME, Bebin EM, Bissler J, Darling TN, de Vries PJ, Frost MD, Fuchs Z, Gosnell ES, Gupta N, Jansen AC. Updated international tuberous sclerosis complex diagnostic criteria and surveillance and management recommendations. Pediatric neurology. 2021 Oct 1;123:50-66.
